basis: Species-specific content sourced from university extension references. Common-name and cultivar records retain separate identification notes.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Philodendron xanadu is a clumping, mounding tropical aroid grown for its deeply divided foliage. NC State describes it as a warm-climate landscape and houseplant, with a dense spreading habit.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Leaves are dark grey-green and deeply divided into many lobes. The plant forms a compact clump rather than a long trailing vine; mature plants can become broad.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Indoors, provide bright indirect light. Outdoors it tolerates sun to partial shade in suitable warm climates, but container foliage should be acclimated gradually to brighter exposure.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water thoroughly, then allow the upper layer of medium to dry before watering again. NC State warns that overwatering can cause yellow leaves.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. Ensure container drainage; avoid prolonged saturation.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: NC State gives 65–75°F (about 18–24°C) as a preferred indoor range. Protect from cold and drafts.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Some humidity is beneficial, but a precise humidity target was not established in the reviewed source. Maintain airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use a balanced houseplant fertilizer during active growth according to label directions. Reduce feeding when growth slows.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove dead or damaged leaves at the base with clean tools. Divide only when a plant has formed separable clumps.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Division is appropriate for established clumps; species-specific propagation detail beyond division was not established in the reviewed source.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State classifies the plant as having low-severity poison characteristics. Keep away from children and pets; do not ingest plant parts.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Overwatering can cause yellowing. No major pest or disease issue was highlighted in the reviewed NC State summary; inspect routinely for common indoor pests.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In warm Dhaka conditions, growth may continue much of the year. Adjust watering to actual drying and drainage, and reduce feeding only when growth slows.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Aglaonema commutatum is a tropical evergreen foliage plant from Southeast Asia. It is commonly grown indoors for its durable leaves and tolerance of lower light.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Plants form upright clumps with simple, oval to lance-shaped leaves. The catalog's plain Aglaonema entry should not be confused with every hybrid cultivar sold as Chinese evergreen.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Low to moderate indirect light is suitable. Avoid strong direct sun, which can scorch leaves; variegated selections may need brighter indirect light to maintain pattern.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the medium moderately moist but allow the top 1–2 inches to dry before watering again. Clemson notes tolerance of some drought but avoid prolonged waterlogging.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a commercial soilless potting mix with added organic matter and reliable drainage. Do not let the pot stand in water.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Clemson recommends about 68–80°F (20–27°C) and avoiding temperatures below 55°F (13°C). Protect from cold drafts.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Aglaonema tolerates lower humidity but prefers moderate humidity. Good airflow is useful in humid climates.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed modestly during active growth with a balanced houseplant fertilizer according to its label. Avoid overfertilizing.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove yellow or damaged leaves at the base using clean tools. Repot when crowded rather than routinely disturbing roots.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Division of established clumps is a practical method; confirm that each division has roots and growing points. Species-specific seed guidance was not established in this source.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: UF/IFAS reports calcium oxalate crystals and low toxicity; all parts may cause dermatitis or internal irritation if ingested. Keep away from pets and children.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Overwatering and cold exposure can cause decline. Watch for common indoor pests; diagnose before treatment.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Maintain moisture checks during hot periods but do not keep the mix constantly saturated. Reduce watering and feeding if growth slows.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Dieffenbachia seguine is an upright tropical aroid grown as a foliage houseplant. Older plants develop a conspicuous cane-like stem.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Leaves are elliptic to oblong and often blotched with cream. NC State notes more than eight prominent lateral veins, often around 20–30, which helps distinguish Dieffenbachia from Aglaonema.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide indirect light or partial shade. Protect from strong direct sunlight.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Water thoroughly, then allow the top inch of soil to dry before watering again. Avoid persistent wetness to reduce root-rot risk.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use loose, fertile, high-organic-matter soil with good drainage. The medium should retain some moisture without remaining saturated.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep in moderate, warm indoor temperatures and protect from cold drafts. The reviewed NC State source does not set a precise optimum range.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: High humidity is tolerated and preferred. Ensure air movement and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Use a balanced houseplant fertilizer during active growth according to label directions; reduce feeding when growth slows.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove damaged lower leaves with clean tools. Wear gloves and avoid contact with sap; wash hands after handling.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: NC State lists division and stem or root cuttings as propagation methods. Use clean tools and handle cut stems carefully.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: Dieffenbachia is toxic and can cause significant irritation if chewed. Keep well away from children and pets; wear gloves and keep sap away from eyes and mouth.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Potential pests include spider mites, scale, whiteflies, fungus gnats and aphids. Diseases include fungal leaf spot, root rot and blight; diagnose before treatment.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka's humid season, prioritize airflow and drainage. Check moisture before watering and remove decaying foliage promptly.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Zamioculcas zamiifolia is a slow-growing, rhizomatous tropical perennial used as a durable indoor foliage plant. Thick rhizomes and fleshy leaf stalks store water.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Upright, arching stems carry glossy, dark green leaflets arranged in pairs along a central rachis. New growth emerges from underground rhizomes.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright indirect light is best, but the plant tolerates very low light. Avoid harsh direct afternoon sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep on the dry side. Water thoroughly, discard runoff, and allow the potting medium to dry well before watering again. Frequent watering in constantly wet soil can cause problems.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a very well-drained potting mix and a container with drainage holes. Avoid oversized pots that remain wet for too long.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Typical warm indoor temperatures are suitable. Protect from cold; the reviewed Iowa State source does not specify a precise range.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Average indoor humidity is tolerated; no special humidity treatment is required by the reviewed source.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Iowa State suggests dilute fertilizer once or twice monthly in spring and summer. Feed only when actively growing and follow product directions; avoid excess salts.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove yellow or damaged stems at the base with clean tools. Avoid unnecessary cutting of healthy foliage.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Propagate by division or leaf cuttings. UConn notes leaf cuttings may take up to nine months to form a rhizome under ordinary household conditions.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: ZZ plant is poisonous if ingested. Calcium oxalate crystals can irritate the mouth and throat; keep away from children and pets.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Few pest or disease problems are reported. Excess water and constantly wet medium are common preventable causes of decline.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In warm Dhaka conditions, allow the medium to dry thoroughly between waterings. Rainy weather and humid air do not mean the rhizome needs more water.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Dracaena trifasciata is an evergreen, clumping succulent-like perennial native to central Africa. It is widely grown as a low-maintenance foliage plant.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Leaves are stiff, upright and sword-shaped, usually with mottled green bands. The species epithet refers to transverse striping. The former name Sansevieria trifasciata is widely encountered.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Bright indirect light is suitable; the plant tolerates low light and some direct sun after acclimation. Avoid abrupt exposure to intense sun.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Allow the soil to dry between waterings. Overwatering can cause root rot; NC State advises very infrequent watering in winter in its temperate context.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a coarse, freely draining succulent mix and a pot with drainage. Avoid dense, moisture-retentive soil.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Warm conditions are preferred, but NC State notes tolerance of cooler temperatures around 50°F (10°C). Protect from frost and prolonged cold.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Low humidity is tolerated. Avoid trapping moisture around the base or keeping foliage wet.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed sparingly during active growth with a diluted balanced fertilizer. Do not routinely fertilize during slow growth.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Remove damaged leaves at soil level with clean tools. Divide crowded clumps when repotting.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Propagate by division or leaf cuttings. Leaf-cutting variegation may not always reproduce the parent pattern in all cultivars.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State identifies low-severity poison characteristics. Keep away from pets and children; ingestion may cause gastrointestinal irritation.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: Overwatering may cause root rot. NC State recommends monitoring for mealybugs and spider mites; significant disease problems are otherwise uncommon.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In Dhaka, shelter from prolonged monsoon rain and ensure pots drain rapidly. Allow the mix to dry before watering again, even in hot weather.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Chlorophytum comosum is a herbaceous perennial from tropical and southern Africa, commonly grown in hanging baskets for its arching foliage and cascading plantlets.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Leaves are narrow and linear, green or striped with white. Long stolons produce small plantlets and flowers, a useful identification feature.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Provide medium, indirect light. It tolerates shade but is intolerant of direct sunlight, which can scorch foliage.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Keep the medium evenly moist during active growth but allow excess water to drain. It tolerates some drying; reduce watering when growth slows.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a standard well-drained potting mix and a container with drainage holes.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep above about 45°F (7°C) and protect from cold. Warm indoor conditions are suitable.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Medium humidity is preferred, although the plant tolerates drier air. Avoid stagnant air.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Avoid overfertilizing, as excess feeding can reduce plantlet formation. Use a balanced fertilizer lightly during active growth.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Trim brown leaf tips or damaged leaves with clean scissors. Remove spent stolons only if plantlets are not wanted.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: Propagate easily by rooting attached or detached plantlets, or by division. Wisconsin Extension notes seed-grown plants may not retain the parent's leaf coloration.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: NC State does not flag this plant as a significant toxicity concern in its profile. Avoid assuming every trade cultivar has been separately toxicologically tested.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: NC State reports no significant pest or disease problems. Brown leaf tips may be associated with water quality or environmental stress; the source notes chlorine and fluoride in tap water can contribute.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: Reduce watering in cooler or slower-growth periods. In Dhaka, monitor pots more often in hot weather but avoid direct balcony sun.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Ficus elastica is an evergreen tropical tree widely grown as an indoor foliage plant. It can become a substantial tree outdoors in suitable frost-free climates.

sections.title: Identification
sections.content: Leaves are large, thick, leathery and glossy, usually elliptic with a prominent midrib. New leaves emerge from a protective sheath; latex sap is present in cut tissue.

sections.title: Light
sections.content: Grow in bright indirect light or partial shade. It can tolerate brighter exposure after gradual acclimation; avoid sudden intense sun indoors.

sections.title: Watering
sections.content: Allow the growing medium to become fairly dry between waterings, especially in containers. Water thoroughly and discard runoff.

sections.title: Soil and drainage
sections.content: Use a well-drained potting medium and a container with open drainage. Avoid keeping roots constantly wet.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.content: Keep warm and protect from cold drafts and frost. The reviewed UF/IFAS profile does not specify an indoor optimum temperature.

sections.title: Humidity
sections.content: Average indoor humidity is generally tolerated; avoid stagnant conditions and maintain airflow.

sections.title: Fertilizing
sections.content: Feed a balanced houseplant fertilizer during active growth according to label directions. Reduce feeding when growth slows.

sections.title: Pruning
sections.content: Prune to control height or remove damaged branches. Wear gloves because cut stems release latex; use clean tools.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.content: UF/IFAS lists propagation by layering or cuttings. Use healthy stem sections and maintain suitable warmth and moisture while rooting.

sections.title: Toxicity and safety
sections.content: Ficus elastica produces latex sap that may irritate skin and eyes. Keep away from children and pets; do not ingest any part.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.content: UF/IFAS notes scale insects may occasionally be a problem; no major pest or disease concerns are listed. Inspect leaf undersides and stems.

sections.title: Seasonal care
sections.content: In warm Dhaka conditions, growth may continue for much of the year. Check moisture frequently during hot periods but avoid waterlogged pots during monsoon weather.

plant-018.identification: This catalog entry uses the common name Chinese evergreen for Aglaonema commutatum. The profile describes the species-level form; many plants sold under the Chinese evergreen name are hybrids with different leaf colors and patterns.

plant-023.identification: ‘Hahnii’ is a dwarf snake-plant cultivar with approximately 6–12 leaves forming a short, funnel-shaped rosette. NC State describes dark green foliage with creamy-white horizontal stripes.
